question.leadin: This city was the projected destination of a 1965 protest march that began in Selma.
question.text: Name this Alabama capital, the site of a bus boycott that began in 1955.
question.clue: This city was the destination of a march, whose participants were attacked by police on "Bloody Sunday" while crossing the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma.

swap.leadin: This Supreme Court case overturned the "separate but equal" doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson.
swap.text: Name this case, in which the Court unanimously ruled that segregation in schools was unconstitutional.
swap.clue: This case's decision cited an experiment in which children were asked to choose between dolls by Kenneth and Mamie Clark.

question.text: King led this organization that fought to end segregation. He founded it with Ralph Abernathy after the Montgomery Bus boycott, and it led a march on Washington.
question.clue: At that time it had been led for four years by Ralph David Abernathy after the death of its founder.

swap.text: This future Supreme Court justice argued before the Court for the NAACP in Brown v. Board of Education.
swap.clue: This person claimed that the most important case he argued as a lawyer was Smith v. Allwright, which made it easier for some people to vote in primaries.

question.text: The White Night Riots took place after the assassination of this first openly gay elected official in the United States, who was shot along with George Moscone by Dan White.
question.clue: This man's death inspired Cleve Jones to begin the NAMES Project.

swap.leadin: This man gave the "Ballot or the Bullet" speech and claimed "We didn't land on Plymouth Rock. The Rock was landed on us."
swap.text: Name this Civil Rights leader, who was assassinated at the Audubon Ballroom in 1965. This activist changed his last name from Little, which he called a "slave master name."
swap.answerHtml: Malcolm X [accept el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz, prompt on Malcolm and X]
swap.clue: This person claimed to receive "spiritual insights" into American racial animosity after observing unity between "blue-eyed blondes" and "black-skinned Africans" during his hajj.

question.leadin: Senator Abraham Ribicoff condemned the police's so-called "Gestapo tactics" during this event.
question.text: Name this event in Chicago where protesters tried to stop Hubert Humphrey's nomination.
question.answerHtml: 1968 Democratic National Convention [or 1968 DNC; prompt on answers describing the Chicago Democratic National Convention or Chicago DNC by asking, “in what year?”]
question.clue: During this event, Abraham Ribicoff denounced "Gestapo tactics on the streets of Chicago."

swap.text: Buckley debated this man on Firing Line in 1968, arguing against his segregationist policies. This man's ticket, with Curtis LeMay, won five states in that year's presidential election.
swap.clue: At Dettingen, a monarch of this name became the last English king to lead troops into battle.

question.leadin: Identify the following about Abe Fortas.
question.text: Fortas was nominated to be Chief Justice by this president, but the nomination was withdrawn due to scandal.
question.clue: This politician was targeted with the chant "How many kids did you kill today?" by protestors opposed to a war that he dramatically escalated after the Gulf of Tonkin Incident.

swap.text: Modified by the "loss of liberty" standard in Argersinger v. Hamlin, it drew on Powell v. Alabama. For 15 points, name this case that incorporated the "right to counsel" clause of the Sixth Amendment, guaranteeing an attorney to anyone accused of a state felony.
swap.clue: Losing attorney Bruce Jacob stated that his strategy in this case was to tie it to Betts v. Brady, which was overturned by this case.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the intersections of sex and politics.
question.text: In 1982, California politician John Schmitz admitted to fathering a baby out of wedlock, which effectively ended his career. Schmitz was the 1972 presidential nominee of the American Independent Party, which in 1968 nominated this conservative for the presidency with running mate Curtis LeMay.
question.clue: This governor from Alabama had earlier run for president and ran again in 1968, resulting in a whopping four attempts to become to president. In the '64 election, he famously said "we will close every highway in the country."

swap.text: Hampton chaired the Illinois chapter of this revolutionary group founded by Bobby Seale and Huey Newton in Oakland. Richard Aoki, a leader of this group, was an FBI informant.
swap.clue: This group, whose members included Fred Hampton, was led by a man arrested for shooting police officer John Frey.

question.leadin: This speech notes "Uncle Sam's hands are dripping with blood. Dripping with the blood of the black man in this country."
question.text: Give this speech delivered less than a month after its speaker's break with the Nation of Islam. This speech was delivered at a Methodist church in Cleveland and advises African Americans to vote for change, but claims it may be necessary to take up arms if injustices continue.
question.clue: This speech that warned of a racial "powder keg" more dangerous than Russian atomic bombs. This speech exhorted African Americans of all faiths to fight for civil rights with either of its two title means.

swap.text: In 1965, Mink introduced the first federal child-care bill to Congress, which was a part of this set of Lyndon Johnson programs that sought to eliminate racial injustice and poverty.
swap.clue: One act under this program significantly boosted public education funding, while another created the Corporation for Public Broadcasting.

question.text: The exclusion of women at the march was protested by this African-American feminist, who had been arrested in 1970 for purchasing a shotgun used in an escape attempt by the Soledad Brothers, though she was acquitted.
question.clue: This former UCLA professor and member of the Black Panthers was put on trial for her alleged role in the attempted kidnapping of Judge Howard Haley at a Marin County courthouse.

swap.text: Previous SNCC chairman Stokely Carmichael first popularized this phrase to replace Martin Luther King's "Freedom Now" slogan. This term is often accompanied by raising a closed fist in salute.
swap.clue: This movement's Abeng group formed after Hugh Shearer ordered Mona's campus to expel the New World Group historian who defined its three aims, Walter Rodney.

question.leadin: Answer the following about affirmative action in the United States.
question.text: This 2003 case held that the University of Michigan had violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by giving minority applicants points because of their race.

swap.leadin: This amendment was championed by groups like NOW and was first proposed in 1923.
swap.text: Identify this un-ratified amendment that called for gender equality.
swap.clue: This legislation failed to pass since only 35 ratified it by 1979.

question.text: This one-time leader of the NAACP spoke at the Prayer Pilgrimage. Under his leadership, the NAACP helped black-owned businesses get loans in the South by backing the Tri-State Bank, and he eventually stepped down in 1977.
question.clue: This activist was leader of the NAACP from 1955 to 1977, succeeding Walter White. He had earlier edited W.E.B. Du Bois's The Crisis magazine, and was known for opposing militancy in the civil rights movement.

swap.text: This two-word phrase coined by Senator Harry Byrd Sr. describes an earlier attempt to subvert desegregation in 1950s Virginia. It was aided by the legislative Stanley Plan, which gave white students grants to attend private academies that sprung up, while entire school districts shut down for years as part of this campaign.
swap.clue: As part of this strategy, a state legislature adopted the Stanley Plan, which created a Pupil Placement Board.
